---
title: Formalization notes for Fermat's Last Theorem
description: Planning notes for the polynomial and regular-prime targets in index.qmd.
---

The [human chapter](index.qmd) describes polynomial proofs by descent, Mason–Stothers, and Riemann–Hurwitz, followed by Kummer's two cases for regular primes. The paired sidecar tracks the targets in that chapter.

The primitive solution predicate uses Bézout coprimality for each pair of coordinates. This expresses that the two coordinates generate the unit ideal. The predicate is defined for any natural exponent, and the subsequent theorems impose their own bounds.

The integer exponent-four result uses Mathlib's `not_fermat_42`. The polynomial proof via Mason–Stothers uses `Polynomial.abc`. The infinite descent proof uses the cyclotomic factorization and a minimal maximum coordinate degree. With $u_0^n = z - x$ and $u_1^n = z - \zeta x$, the difference $u_1^n - u_0^n$ equals $(1 - \zeta)x$.

For the cyclotomic coprimality statement, the allowed positive-characteristic case requires interpreting the coefficient ring generated by the root of unity as the image of the integer evaluation map. Keep the comparison with the characteristic-zero cyclotomic integers explicit when using it in Kummer's argument.

For the [prime-power congruence](index.qmd#lem-pth-power-congruence), first lift the residue of $\alpha$ to an integer $r$. Choose $a=r^p$ for the two congruences modulo $\lambda^p$. Fermat's little theorem gives $a\equiv r\pmod{\lambda}$, and raising to the $p$-th power lifts this last congruence to $\lambda^p$.

::: {#thm-dedekind-weil-divisor}
## Fractional ideals and Weil divisors

For the [Dedekind domain recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), index Weil divisors by the nonzero prime ideals of a Dedekind domain $R$. The exponent of a prime in a nonzero fractional ideal gives an integer. These exponents have finite support, add under ideal multiplication, and recover the ideal by taking the product of prime powers. This defines the group isomorphism for Weil divisors. In the field case the index set is empty and the group is trivial.
:::

::: {#lem-dedekind-principal-order}
## Local orders of principal ideals

In the [Dedekind domain recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), the order of a nonzero rational function at a nonzero prime equals the prime exponent of the principal fractional ideal it generates. Mathlib writes the valuation multiplicatively. The exponential of the negative ideal exponent gives that multiplicative valuation.
:::

::: {#prp-dedekind-spectrum-local-rings}
## Points and local rings of an affine Dedekind scheme

For the [Dedekind domain recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), the generic point is the zero prime, and its residue field is canonically the fraction field. Every other point is closed and has a discrete valuation ring as its stalk. When the coordinate ring is a field, the generic point is also closed and its stalk is a field. At a nonzero prime the order on the stalk, expressed multiplicatively, is the inverse adic valuation on the fraction field. Taking its logarithm gives the usual additive order.
:::

For the [Picard group comparison](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), the height-one primes correspond to codimension-one points, with matching orders on rational functions. If $D_I$ records the prime exponents of a fractional ideal $I$, then the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O(-D_I)$ has $I$ as its global rational sections. Its class is the image of $[I]$ under the isomorphism $\operatorname{Cl}(R)\cong\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}R)$.

::: {#thm-fermat-function-field-genus}
## Genus of the Fermat function field

For the [Fermat genus calculation](index.qmd#prp-fermat-genus), let $F = k(x,y)$ with $x$ transcendental over a field $k$ of characteristic zero and $x^n + y^n = 1$ for $n > 0$. The homogeneous Fermat polynomial has no common nonzero zero of its partial derivatives over an algebraic closure. Tau Ceti's plane curve genus theorem gives $g(F) = (n-1)(n-2)/2$ and shows that $k$ is the exact constant field. For the [geometric Fermat theorem](index.qmd#thm-flt-geometric), the normalized coordinates would put this field inside $k(t)$, which has genus zero. Riemann–Hurwitz excludes that inclusion when $n \ge 3$.
:::

::: {#def-fermat-projective-scheme}
## The projective Fermat scheme

For the [projective Fermat curve](index.qmd#prp-fermat-genus), take the homogeneous quotient of $k[X,Y,Z]$ by $(X^n+Y^n-Z^n)$ and form its projective spectrum. This gives a closed subscheme of $\mathbb{P}^2_k$ and a proper morphism to $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Its three coordinate opens cover it. Over algebraically closed constants of characteristic zero and for $n>0$, dehomogenizing at $Z$ preserves degree and yields an irreducible equation, so the homogeneous coordinate ring is a domain and the projective scheme is integral.
:::

::: {#prp-fermat-projective-smooth}
## Smooth charts of the projective Fermat scheme

For the [projective Fermat curve](index.qmd#prp-fermat-genus), the degree-zero localization at each coordinate identifies with the quotient by the corresponding dehomogenized polynomial. A polynomial in two variables can be homogenized to prove surjectivity. For injectivity, homogenize the multiple of the dehomogenized equation and cancel powers of the inverted coordinate using primality of the homogeneous equation. The polynomial and its two partial derivatives generate the unit ideal in each chart, so the Jacobian criterion gives smoothness of relative dimension one on the projective scheme.
:::

The function field of the projective Fermat curve is the fraction field of the $Z\ne0$ chart. Its normalized coordinates satisfy $x^n+y^n=1$ and generate the field over $k$. The curve is smooth, integral, and proper of dimension one. The comparison of its scheme genus with its function-field genus gives $\dim_k H^1(F_n,\mathcal O_{F_n})=(n-1)(n-2)/2$.

::: {#prp-plane-jacobian-criterion}
## The projective plane Jacobian criterion

For the [projective curve recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-curves-recall), the standard opens of the projective plane are spectra of polynomial rings in two variables. On the corresponding opens of a homogeneous hypersurface, the chart rings are the quotients by the dehomogenized equation. The affine derivative opens are smooth of relative dimension one. The Euler relation transfers projective nonvanishing of a derivative to these charts, including in positive characteristic. Conversely, formal smoothness splits the conormal map of the affine hypersurface and forces some derivative to survive at every point of the equation over the algebraically closed field. For a nonzero equation of positive degree, the no-common-zero condition gives an integral proper curve of dimension one and discrete valuation rings at its closed points.
:::

::: {#lem-curve-extension-and-infinity-coordinates}
## Extension from a dense open and coordinates at infinity

For the [projective curve recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-curves-recall), a morphism into a proper scheme extends uniquely from a dense open of an integral curve with discrete valuation rings at its codimension-one points. On the chart at infinity, if $M$ is the maximum coordinate degree, the reflected polynomials $s^M p_i(s^{-1})$ generate the unit ideal and satisfy the same homogeneous equations. A leading coefficient gives a nonzero coordinate at $s=0$.

For a homogeneous hypersurface over a field, the affine morphisms from the original and reflected tuples agree on the overlap of the two charts. Their tuples differ there by a common unit. The reflected tuple therefore describes the restriction of the projective extension to the chart at infinity, including its value at $s=0$.

For a nonconstant map to a plane curve of degree $n$, the coordinates give a pullback of $\mathcal O_C(1)$ of degree $M$. Since $\deg\mathcal O_C(1)=n$, the map degree satisfies $M=n\deg\pi$. For a direct map to $\mathbb P^1$ the corresponding line bundle has degree one.
:::

::: {#prp-fermat-line-morphism}
## The morphism from polynomial coordinates

For the [projective curve recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-curves-recall), polynomial coordinates that generate the unit ideal and satisfy the homogeneous Fermat equation define a morphism from the affine line to the projective Fermat scheme. The inverse image of each coordinate open is the basic open of its coordinate polynomial. The affine morphism extends uniquely over the projective line, and on the chart at infinity its coordinates are the reflected polynomials. On the overlap the two coordinate systems differ by a common unit.
:::

::: {#prp-fermat-line-morphism-degree}
## Degree of the polynomial-coordinate Fermat morphism

Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, and let $n>0$. If a polynomial Fermat tuple generates the unit ideal and has maximum coordinate degree $M>0$, the induced morphism $\pi\colon\mathbb P^1_k\to F_n$ is dominant. At the generic point, the last coordinate is nonzero and the affine chart identifies the image of $\pi^*$ on function fields with the field generated by $a=x/z$ and $b=y/z$. The reduced ratio $a$ gives a projection of degree $M$. Over $k(a)$, the coordinate $b$ has degree $n$, from the irreducible affine equation $b^n=1-a^n$. The tower formula then gives $M=n\deg\pi$ for the actual function-field map of $\pi$.
:::

::: {#prp-plane-line-morphism-degree}
## Degree of the polynomial-coordinate map to a smooth plane curve

For the [projective curve recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-curves-recall), take a nonzero homogeneous equation of degree $d>0$ defining a smooth plane curve over an algebraically closed field. A polynomial tuple satisfying the equation, generating the unit ideal, and having maximum coordinate degree $M>0$ extends uniquely to a dominant morphism $\pi$ from the projective line. Choose a nonzero denominator among the coordinates and use its affine chart. On the target, the supremum of the pole divisors of the two coordinate ratios has degree $d$. On $k(t)$ its pullback is the zero divisor of the denominator plus the difference between $M$ and the denominator's degree at infinity. Its degree is therefore $M$. Conorm multiplies the divisor degree by the degree of the actual function-field extension, so $M=d\deg\pi$. The argument also applies to lines and tuples with a zero coordinate.
:::

::: {#thm-tame-hurwitz-function-fields}
## Canonical divisors and tame Riemann–Hurwitz

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), use divisors of Weil differentials over algebraically closed constants of characteristic zero. The canonical divisor has degree $2g-2$. Pulling it to the extension adds the tame different, whose coefficient at a place is $e_P-1$. Every place has degree one. For a genus-zero cover of degree $d$, the preimage of a set of $s$ places therefore has at least $sd-(2d-2)$ places.
:::

::: {#lem-tame-relative-differential-length}
## Length of the local relative differentials

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), write the image of the source uniformizer as $\varepsilon\pi^e$ in the target discrete valuation ring. If $e$ is a unit in the residue field, the differential is $\pi^{e-1}$ times a unit times $d\pi$. Under the local smoothness hypotheses, the uniformizer differential generates the absolute differential module by the cotangent sequence and Nakayama’s lemma. Transitivity then presents the relative differential module as the quotient by the $(e-1)$st power of the maximal ideal, so it has length $e-1$.
:::

::: {#prp-differential-sheaf-transitivity}
## Transitivity of relative differential sheaves

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), adjunction gives the map $f^*\Omega_{Y/k}\to\Omega_{X/k}$. Its cokernel represents derivations on $X$ that annihilate every local function pulled back from $Y$. This identifies the cokernel as $\Omega_{X/Y}$ and yields the right-exact transitivity sequence $f^*\Omega_{Y/k}\to\Omega_{X/k}\to\Omega_{X/Y}\to 0$.
:::

::: {#prp-scalar-extension-of-stalks}
## Scalar extension on stalks of pullback sheaves

For a morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ and an $\mathcal O_Y$-module $M$, the stalk $(f^*M)_x$ identifies with $\mathcal O_{X,x}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}}M_{f(x)}$. This follows by applying the pullback adjunction to skyscraper modules at $x$. For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), this identification sends the first map of the sheaf transitivity sequence on stalks to the first map of Kähler transitivity for the local rings.
:::

::: {#prp-differential-pullback-on-stalks}
## Pullback of differentials on stalks and at places

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), the sheaf morphism $\Omega_{Y/k}\to f_*\Omega_{X/k}$ induces the Kähler differential map of the local ring homomorphism after identifying the stalk modules. The local transitivity calculation then applies to the actual stalk rings. For places of a finite function-field extension, the normalized discrete valuation of a pulled-back uniformizer is the place ramification index. The corresponding relative differential length is $e-1$ under the local smoothness hypotheses.
:::

::: {#prp-relative-differential-sheaf-stalks}
## Local modules of the relative differential sheaf

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), taking the stalk at $x$ is left adjoint to the skyscraper construction and preserves cokernels. Taking the cokernel of the first Kähler map therefore identifies $(\Omega_{X/Y})_x$ with $\Omega_{\mathcal O_{X,x}/\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}}$. This identification sends the sheaf quotient map to the Kähler quotient map. Under the local discrete valuation and differential hypotheses, the length of the relative sheaf stalk is $e_x-1$.
:::

::: {#prp-differential-sheaf-short-exact}
## Injectivity of the differential pullback for curves

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), a dominant morphism of integral curves over a field of characteristic zero induces a finite separable extension of function fields. The pullback map on differentials at the generic point is an isomorphism after extending scalars. When the target is smooth of relative dimension one, its differential sheaf is a line bundle and so is its pullback. Each section of the pulled-back line bundle is determined by its generic germ on a nonempty open. The first differential map is therefore injective, giving the short exact transitivity sequence.
:::

::: {#prp-closed-curve-differential-length}
## Relative differential length at closed curve points

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), consider a dominant morphism of smooth integral curves over a characteristic-zero field. At a closed point $x$, the local rings at $x$ and $f(x)$ are discrete valuation rings, and both absolute differential modules are free of rank one. The residue fields are finite separable extensions of the base and have zero relative differentials. Dominance gives injectivity of the local ring map. The length of $(\Omega_{X/Y})_x$ is $e_x-1$, and the stalk is nonzero exactly when $e_x>1$. In any bases of the pulled-back and target differential stalks, the first sheaf arrow is multiplication by a scalar. Its order is the length of the quotient by that scalar, hence also $e_x-1$.
:::

::: {#prp-cartier-ramification-divisor}
## The Cartier ramification divisor and the canonical sheaf

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), the injective morphism $f^*\Omega_{Y/k}\to\Omega_{X/k}$ between line bundles defines an effective Cartier divisor $R_f$ by its local multipliers. The target bundle is isomorphic to the source bundle tensored with $\mathcal O_X(R_f)$. At a closed point the order of a local equation is the relative differential length. The place of that point restricts to the place of its image, and the local ring ramification index agrees with the normalized function-field index. Thus the Weil divisor of $R_f$ is the tame different transported to the curve, and its associated Weil divisor sheaf gives the same twist.
:::

::: {#prp-relative-differential-skyscrapers}
## The relative differential sheaf as a finite product

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), separability makes the generic relative differential stalk zero. At a closed point the stalk is nonzero exactly when the ramification index exceeds one. These points are the finite support of the ramification divisor. On an open set, any tuple of germs at the supported points has representatives on neighbourhoods that exclude the other supported points. The representatives glue because agreement can be checked at stalks. This identifies the relative differential sheaf with the finite product of its stalk skyscrapers via the germ maps.
:::

::: {#prp-canonical-differential-degrees}
## Canonical sheaf degrees and the ramification twist

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), a smooth proper integral curve over a perfect field exact in its function field has $\dim_k H^0(X,\Omega_{X/k})=g(X)$ and $\deg\Omega_{X/k}=2g(X)-2$. The Euler degree of the canonical sheaf is the sum of the degree of the pulled-back canonical sheaf and the residue-weighted degree of the Weil ramification divisor. In characteristic zero with exact constants on both curves, the degree of the pulled-back canonical sheaf is the degree of the function-field extension times that of the target canonical sheaf. Over algebraically closed constants all residue weights are one.

In the algebraically closed case the correction term is the sum of the actual local ring indices minus one over the support of the Weil ramification divisor. A codimension-one point belongs to the support exactly when its local index exceeds one.

A morphism of proper integral curves with two distinct image points is dominant and proper. Each fibre is finite, so the morphism is finite by Zariski's main theorem. Its image is closed and dense, hence it is surjective.
:::

::: {#prp-projective-line-canonical-differential}
## The canonical differential of the projective line

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), the two polynomial charts make the projective line smooth of relative dimension one. Its function field is $k(t)$, and its genus is zero. At the point outside the affine chart, $s=t^{-1}$ has order one and $dt=-s^{-2}ds$. The divisor of the rational differential $dt$ is $-2[\infty]$ in characteristic zero. Its divisor sheaf identifies with the canonical sheaf, whose degree is $-2$.
:::

::: {#thm-tame-hurwitz-schemes}
## The numerical Riemann–Hurwitz formula for schemes

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), a dominant morphism of proper regular curves over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero gives a finite extension of their function fields. The scheme genus $\dim_k H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$ agrees with the function-field genus. Codimension-one points correspond to places, so the degree of the tame different becomes the sum of $e_P-1$ over the ramified points of the source. This gives the numerical formula for the actual scheme morphism.
:::

In the [Mason–Hurwitz argument](index.qmd#rem-mason-hurwitz-bridge), the point at infinity of the source contributes to the three fibres if its image is $0$, $1$, or $\infty$. This gives the stated upper bound of the radical degree plus one.

::: {#lem-kummer-local-congruence}
## Local congruences for Kummer’s unit lemma

For the [proof of Kummer’s unit lemma](index.qmd#rem-kummer-unit-proof), suppose $u$ is congruent to an integer modulo $p$. Fermat’s little theorem gives $u^{p-1}=1+pb$ with $b$ integral. Since $p$ is odd, the norm of $u^{p-1}$ is one. Expanding the norm modulo $p^2$ shows that $p$ divides the trace of $b$. Every conjugate of $b$ has the same residue modulo $\lambda$, so the trace reduces to $(p-1)b$. Thus $\lambda$ divides $b$ and $\lambda^p$ divides $u^{p-1}-1$.

Set $U=u^{p-1}$ and take $r^p=U$. Dividing $(\lambda X+1)^p-U$ coefficientwise by $\lambda^p$ gives a monic integral polynomial vanishing at $(r-1)/\lambda$.

For $p=3$, the congruence hypothesis implies $u=\pm1$ by Mathlib’s classification of cubic cyclotomic units congruent to integers modulo $\lambda^2$. Cubing the six units $\pm\zeta_3^j$ gives exactly the two values $\pm1$.
:::

::: {#lem-kummer-extension-unramified}
## Unramifiedness of the Kummer extension

For the [proof of Kummer’s unit lemma](index.qmd#rem-kummer-unit-proof), a nontrivial automorphism of $K(r)/K$ sends $r$ to $\zeta_p^j r$ with $1\le j<p$. Its difference on the integral element $(r-1)/\lambda$ is $((\zeta_p^j-1)/\lambda)r$. The first factor is a cyclotomic unit, and $r$ is an integral unit because $r^p=U$. The difference is a unit, so it cannot vanish modulo any proper prime ideal. This makes the inertia group trivial at every finite prime.
:::

For the class-number step of the [unit lemma](index.qmd#lem-kummer-unit), a cyclic extension of degree $d$ supplies all $d$th powers as idèle-class norms. If $d$ is coprime to the class number, each idèle class is a product of such a power and a class represented by local units at every finite place. Unramifiedness makes these local units norms, and all infinite places of the base are complex. The first fundamental inequality then forces $d=1$. Thus $U=u^{p-1}$ has a $p$th root $r$ in $K$, and $u/r$ and its inverse are integral because their $p$th powers are integral units.

::: {#prp-bernoulli-numerator-test-below-100}
## Bernoulli numerator tests below 100

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), among odd primes below 100, some numerator in $B_2,B_4,\ldots,B_{p-3}$ is divisible by $p$ exactly for $37$, $59$, and $67$. The witnesses are $B_{32}$, $B_{44}$, and $B_{58}$, respectively. Lean checks the finite table using Mathlib’s rational Bernoulli recurrence.
:::

::: {#lem-bernoulli-kummer-congruence}
## The first Kummer congruence at coprime even indices

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), let $p\ge5$ be prime. For positive even indices $m,n$ prime to $p$ and congruent modulo $p-1$, with $p-1$ dividing neither index, the difference $B_m/m-B_n/n$ is divisible by $p$ in the ring of $p$-integral rationals. Von Staudt–Clausen bounds the denominators in Faulhaber's formula. Multiplying residues by a primitive root and expanding modulo $p^2$ gives the congruence, which transfers numerator divisibility between the two indices.
:::

::: {#thm-bernoulli-irregular-infinite}
## Infinitely many primes satisfying the Bernoulli numerator test

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), Jensen's argument begins with a finite set $S$ of primes satisfying the numerator test and a prime $q$ larger than every element of $S$, with $q\equiv1\pmod{12\prod_{p\in S}p(p-1)}$. The denominator of $B_{2q}$ is six. Euler's formula for even zeta values gives positivity, and Faulhaber's formula at four gives a numerator congruent to three modulo four. A prime divisor $p\equiv3\pmod4$ of that numerator is different from $q$ and is at least five. Reducing $2q$ modulo $p-1$ and using Kummer's congruence gives an even irregular index between two and $p-3$. For a prime in $S$, the reduced index would be two, whose Bernoulli numerator is one. Thus the numerator test holds for infinitely many primes, even within the residue class three modulo four.

The relative class-number formula sends each of these primes to a divisor of the full class number of its cyclotomic field. Hence infinitely many primes congruent to three modulo four are irregular in the class-number sense.
:::

::: {#prp-cyclotomic-class-number-reduction}
## Class numbers and zeta residues of a prime cyclotomic field

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), let $K$ be a prime cyclotomic field of odd conductor $p$ and let $K^+$ be its maximal real subfield. Extension of ideal classes followed by relative norm is squaring. By Cauchy's theorem, $p$ divides the class number of $K$ precisely when it divides the class number of $K^+$ or the order of the relative norm kernel. The cyclotomic real-unit index is one and the torsion has order $2p$. The primitive root $\zeta$ generates the integer ring over that of $K^+$, and the derivative $\zeta-\zeta^{-1}$ generates the relative different of absolute norm $p$. The discriminant tower and analytic class-number formula give the quotient of the two Dedekind-zeta residues as $(2\pi)^m/(2p\sqrt{p^m})$ times the class-number ratio, where $m=(p-1)/2$.
:::

::: {#prp-teichmuller-bernoulli-factors}
## The ordinary numerator test for the Teichmüller factors

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), write $\omega$ for the $p$-adic Teichmüller character. For odd $i$, $p B_{1,\omega^i}$ is the weighted sum $\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}a\omega(a)^i$. Each Teichmüller lift is congruent to $a^p$ modulo $p^2$. For $i+1<p-1$, Faulhaber's formula and Kummer's congruence identify divisibility of this sum by $p^2$ with divisibility of the numerator of $B_{i+1}$ by $p$. At the exceptional exponent $i=p-2$, the weighted sum reduces to $-1$ modulo $p$, so $B_{1,\omega^{p-2}}$ has valuation $-1$.

The character $\omega$ is odd and has order $p-1$. The normalized product $p\prod_{1\le i<p-1,\ i\text{ odd}} B_{1,\omega^i}$ is a $p$-adic integer. The exceptional factor uses the prefactor $p$ and becomes a unit. The normalized product is divisible by $p$ precisely when an ordinary numerator in the irregularity range is divisible by $p$.
:::

::: {#prp-odd-bernoulli-product-transport}
## The odd Bernoulli product over the complex and p-adic fields

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), every character modulo $p$ is defined over $\mathbb Q(\mu_{p-1})$. Its embeddings into $\mathbb C$ and $\mathbb Q_p$ carry the full odd Bernoulli product to the corresponding products over those fields. An integer equal to the normalized complex product times $\pm d/2^a$, with $p\nmid d$, is divisible by $p$ precisely when the ordinary numerator test holds. For the relative class-number identity, the class-group norm cokernel has order prime to $p$ because the relative extension is quadratic. This gives the exact numerator criterion for the norm kernel assuming the complex relative class-number formula.
:::

::: {#prp-dirichlet-l-values-at-zero}
## Dirichlet L-values and first generalized Bernoulli numbers

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), the logarithm series on the unit circle gives the sine series at exponent one. Summation by parts supplies a summable bound near that exponent, so the sine zeta has value $\pi(1/2-a)$ at one for $0<a<1$. Its functional equation gives $\zeta(0,a)=1/2-a$. Expansion over residue classes then gives $L(0,\chi)=-B_{1,\chi}$ for each nontrivial complex Dirichlet character.
:::

::: {#thm-cyclotomic-relative-class-number}
## The relative class number and the Bernoulli criterion

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), the Euler factors of the full cyclotomic field and its maximal real subfield agree at the conductor. At any other prime their quotient is the product of local factors of the odd characters, by the order of Frobenius. Absolute convergence gives the corresponding quotient of zeta functions and continuity gives the ratio of residues at one. The odd functional equation and the Gauss sum of modulus $\sqrt p$ express the absolute value of each odd $L(1,\chi)$ as $\pi/\sqrt p$ times the modulus of the first Bernoulli number of the inverse character.

Writing $m=(p-1)/2$ and $h,h^+$ for the two class numbers, comparison with the explicit residue ratio gives
$$2^{m-1}h=h^+ p\left|\prod_{\chi\ \mathrm{odd}}B_{1,\chi}\right|.$$
The product is real by conjugation. Transport to the $p$-adic coefficient field and the norm cokernel calculation identify divisibility of the relative class norm kernel with the ordinary Bernoulli test. Consequently $p\mid h$ precisely when $p\mid h^+$ or the Bernoulli test holds. Removing the real-class-number alternative requires the reflection implication.
:::

::: {#prp-integral-fermat-sections}
## Integral sections and primitive Fermat coordinates

For the [arithmetic surface recall](index.qmd#rem-arithmetic-surface), a triple satisfying the Fermat equation and generating the unit ideal gives a section of the integral Fermat scheme. Conversely, restrict a section to the rational generic point, normalize a coordinate to one on a standard chart, and clear denominators with a primitive tuple. Separatedness identifies the reconstructed section with the original. Two primitive integral tuples define the same section exactly when they differ by a common sign. Zero coordinates are allowed, as in $(1,0,1)$ for positive exponents.
:::

::: {#prp-fermat-cone-integral}
## The Fermat cone and the cyclotomic factors

For the [arithmetic surface recall](index.qmd#rem-arithmetic-surface), the homogeneous Fermat coordinate ring over algebraically closed characteristic-zero coefficients is a domain in every positive degree. The geometric generic Fermat cone is therefore integral. The cyclotomic identity factors $X^p+Y^p$ as $\prod_j(X+\zeta_p^jY)$ for odd $p$. Evaluating that identity on a primitive solution gives an ideal factorization with $p$th powers away from the prime over $p$.
:::

::: {#prp-cyclotomic-differentials}
## Differentials of the prime cyclotomic integers

For the [arithmetic surface recall](index.qmd#rem-arithmetic-surface), write $B=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$ and $\lambda=1-\zeta_p$. In the monogenic presentation of $B$, $d\zeta_p$ generates the module of relative differentials with relation $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)d\zeta_p=0$. Differentiating $(X-1)\Phi_p(X)=X^p-1$ shows that $(\zeta_p-1)\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=p\zeta_p^{p-1}$. The derivative therefore generates $(\lambda^{p-2})$, which is also the different ideal. For odd $p$, the cover is étale precisely at primes of $B$ away from $p$.
:::

::: {#prp-cyclotomic-cover-scheme}
## The cyclotomic cover over the integer spectrum

For the [arithmetic surface recall](index.qmd#rem-arithmetic-surface), the structural morphism from the spectrum of a number ring to $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ is finite and flat. Over the basic open $D(p)$, the prime cyclotomic morphism is the spectrum map of $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]\to B[1/p]$. For odd $p$, this map is étale by the differential computation.
:::
